## Summer 2026 Pre-Assignment

**Part 1: R Basics for Development Data**

**Estimated time:** 1.5-3 hours

This first assignment is a bridge from the website warm-up into the real Posit
Cloud work. You will practice the habits that will appear in every later part:
read the prompt, run a small piece of code, check the output, explain what
happened, and knit the file.

## Before you start: bridge from the website

You should be working in your own saved copy of the Posit Cloud project. If you
do not remember doing that, stop and return to the Getting Started page on the
course website before editing this file.

Use the Files pane to confirm that you opened:

```text
assignments/R Summer Assignment 1.Rmd
```

This `.Rmd` file is where your code and short written answers belong. Knitted
HTML may help you preview your work, but you submit the completed `.Rmd` file.

## Learning goals

By the end of Part 1, you should be able to:

- run R code in a chunk;
- create objects with `<-`;
- use comments to explain code;
- identify basic data types;
- use logical checks;
- use basic functions;
- create vectors;
- read and fix a simple error message; and
- explain why knitting checks reproducibility.

## Why this matters for API-209 and MPA/ID

API-209 uses data to reason carefully about policy questions. Before using
models, graphs, or development indicators, you need a few reliable habits:
write code you understand, check what R returned, and explain results in words
without overclaiming. This assignment is about those habits.

## Lesson 2: Data types

### Goal

Recognize the difference between numbers and text values.

### Concept

R works with different kinds of values. Numbers are numeric values. Words inside
quotation marks are character values.

```{r}

"Harvard Kennedy School"
"Ghana"
```

## Lesson 3: Logical values

### Goal

Use `TRUE` and `FALSE` checks, which are the foundation of filtering data.

### Concept

Logical values are `TRUE` or `FALSE`. The operator `==` asks whether two things
are equal. The operator `!=` asks whether two things are not equal.

### Try it

```{r}
3 == 3
2 == 4
"Ghana" == "Kenya"
```

```{r}
"Ghana" != "Kenya"
2024 != 2023
```

## Lesson 4: Objects

### Goal

Create named objects and reuse them in calculations and checks.

### Concept

Objects store values so you can use them later. The assignment operator `<-`
puts the value on the right into the name on the left.

### Try it

```{r}
country <- "Ghana"
year <- 2023
population <- 33787914
```

Run the object names to see what they store:

```{r}
country
year
population
```

Use objects in calculations:

```{r}
population_millions <- population / 1000000
population_millions
```

Use objects in logical checks:

```{r}
country == "Ghana"
year >= 2020
```

## Lesson 5: Functions and vectors

### Goal

Use functions and vectors to summarize several values.

### Concept

Functions perform tasks. Most functions use parentheses. A vector stores
several values in one object. Use `c()` to combine values.

### Try it

```{r}
sqrt(9)
log(100)
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

The values inside parentheses are called arguments. Some arguments are required;
others are optional.

```{r}
mean(c(10, 20, 30))
max(c(10, 20, 30))
min(c(10, 20, 30))
```

Now create two vectors:

```{r}
peer_countries <- c("Ghana", "Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania")
growth_rates <- c(3.8, 5.6, 8.2, 5.1)
```

Run the objects:

```{r}
peer_countries
growth_rates
mean(growth_rates)
growth_rates > 5
```
